title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Dust and Desire: The Novel's Opening Architecture

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate, sometimes argumentative look at one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and today we begin at the beginning — with the novel's opening architecture, the world Dickens builds before a single plot has properly turned.
Dust heaps, river mist, a foggy London that barely exists — this is the atmosphere Dickens conjures, and it is extraordinary.
Joining me today are three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing something quite distinct to the table.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who obsesses, in the best possible way, over how great prose actually works — the architecture of sentences, the structural choices that create meaning.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about what the world of this novel actually was — the institutions, the poverty, the law.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and cares, above all, about the experience of reading it — what moves you, what makes you stop and re-read a sentence.
Let's start with the dust — because everything in this novel, in a sense, starts with the dust.
The dust heaps are announced to us through Mortimer Lightwood, who is telling the story of John Harmon's father at a dinner party — which is itself a remarkable framing choice.
Dickens is making the exposition theatrical — we're hearing this as gossip, as entertainment, almost as a set-piece performance.
And then Mortimer describes the old Dust Contractor's estate, and the language just — accumulates.
Listen to how Dickens builds the list:
"Coal-dust, vegetable-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust, rough dust and sifted dust,—all manner of Dust."
The capitalised final "Dust" — that's not carelessness, that's a declaration.
Dust becomes a category, almost a deity — the governing principle of this entire world.
And every item in that list — coal, vegetable, bone, crockery — is waste, is the residue of consumption.
It's worth being precise about what dust heaps actually were, because it sharpens the satire considerably.
In mid-Victorian London, dust contractors collected the city's ash and refuse — the "dust" from domestic hearths primarily — and sorted it for resale.
The cinders went to brickmakers, the finer ash as fertiliser — these were enormously profitable operations.

So when Dickens writes that the old man "grew rich as a Dust Contractor, and lived in a hollow in a hilly country entirely composed of Dust" — that is a factually grounded description of a known type of Victorian wealth.
The fortune is real; the absurdity is real; the moral indictment is real.
Dickens describes him as throwing up "his own mountain range, like an old volcano" — the geological metaphor giving this petty profiteer the scale of a geological force.
That is not accidental flattery — it is savage irony.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the comedy of it — the sheer comic relish with which Dickens piles on the categories of dust.
It reads like a parody of a merchant's inventory — "rough dust and sifted dust" — as though there is a quality hierarchy even in waste.
But then Dickens does something that I find quietly devastating — he contrasts all this accumulated wealth with where Gaffer Hexam actually lives.
The description of Hexam's old mill-house is one of the most brilliantly uncomfortable passages in the opening chapters.
Everything in it is described in terms of decay:
"roof, and walls, and floor, alike abounding in old smears of flour, red-lead, and damp, alike had a look of decomposition."
"A look of decomposition" — that phrase does not let you go.
Caroline is absolutely right to put those two environments side by side — the satire of wealth and the exposure of poverty are doing the same structural work.
Notice how Dickens describes the mill-house with the same cumulative technique — "This, being very old, knotted, seamed, and beamed" — the list enacts the very texture of the place.
And then there's the lamp — "a common lamp, shaped like a hyacinth-root, smoked and flared in the neck of a stone bottle on the table."
The hyacinth-root is extraordinary — it's grotesque but also somehow organic, alive, as if poverty itself has grown this strange shape.
Dickens is building his atmosphere out of specific, unglamorous objects — and that specificity is what makes it real, and therefore terrible.
The setting carries legal weight too — there is nothing accidental about Gaffer Hexam living in a building that looks like it is already dissolving.
People living on the margins of the river economy in 1860s London occupied exactly this kind of condemned, semi-derelict space — legally ambiguous, physically precarious.
The scattered oars, the clumsy stair "little better than a ladder" — these details locate Hexam in a specific class of river worker for whom the Thames was simultaneously workplace and grave.
And Dickens understood that the atmosphere of such a place was not separable from the economic conditions that created it.
And Dickens extends this atmospheric instinct to the whole city — there's a fog passage later in the novel that I find almost hallucinatory in its power.
He describes London on a foggy day as a city that has almost ceased to exist.

"Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither."
"Divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither" — that is an impossibly good sentence.
London is not hidden by the fog — it is ontologically suspended.
What I love about that passage is the gradation — Dickens actually maps the colour of the fog as you move toward the City.
"Dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City — it was rusty-black."
That is topographical realism and moral symbolism in the same breath — the closer you get to the centre of money, the darker the air.
And then the sun itself — "showed as if it had gone out and were collapsing flat and cold."
A collapsing sun is not meteorology — it is cosmology.
And this atmospheric instinct reaches its most concentrated form in the river passages — particularly the dawn at Plashwater Weir.
The Thames in this novel is not a picturesque backdrop — it is the engine of the plot, the place where bodies are found and fortunes are made.
And Dickens renders it with this extraordinary economy of phrase:
"the trees were the ghosts of trees, and the water was the ghost of water."
Five words — "the water was the ghost" — and the Thames has become something between a place and an idea.
The economy of that is stunning — and it tells us that Dickens is not writing about the river as landscape but as state of being.
That phrase — "the water was the ghost of water" — is the kind of line that sends you back to the beginning of the novel and reconfigures everything.
Because the novel opens on the river — Gaffer Hexam out on the dark water, dragging for bodies — and this ghostly dawn closes a long loop.
The river is where identity dissolves, where the dead return, where money begins.
And Dickens signals all of that in a single, perfectly balanced five-word clause.
Dust, fog, ghost-water — Dickens has laid out his entire moral and atmospheric vocabulary in the novel's opening movements, and we've barely met the characters yet.

In our next segment, we'll turn to the characters themselves — the Veneerings, Bella Wilfer, the Boffins — and ask what Dickens is doing with identity and reinvention in a world built on inherited waste.

segments.title: Money and Morality: Reading Bella's Greed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — sentence by sentence, scene by scene.
I'm your host, and today we have three brilliant readers around the table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks about novels the way an architect thinks about cathedrals — from the inside out.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what poverty meant in Dickens's England — and isn't shy about the anger that knowledge brings.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and can tell you precisely which sentences stop you cold.
Today's segment is called Money and Morality: Reading Bella's Greed.
Bella Wilfer is one of the most startling heroines in all of Victorian fiction — openly mercenary, hilariously self-aware, and yet somehow redeemable.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because Bella arrives on the page with a complaint that is almost operatic in its fury.
She really does arrive with a kind of magnificent indignation.
What strikes me every time I read this passage is how Dickens lets Bella damn herself entirely in her own voice — and somehow makes you love her for it.
She's complaining about the Harmon arrangement — being left to a stranger in a will — and Dickens gives her this extraordinary riff.
"It was ridiculous enough to have a stranger coming over to marry me, whether he liked it or not.
It was ridiculous enough to know what an embarrassing meeting it would be, and how we never could pretend to have an inclination of our own, either of us.
It was ridiculous enough to know I shouldn't like him — how could I like him, left to him in a will, like a dozen of spoons, with everything cut and dried beforehand, like orange chips."
A dozen of spoons. Orange chips. She reduces herself to household goods — and Dickens knows exactly how funny and how devastating that is.
And then she says it plainly: 'I love money, and want money — want it dreadfully.'
That triple repetition of 'ridiculous enough' is doing so much work.
It's an anaphora — a rhetorical device Dickens reaches for when a character is spinning out of control — and it mimics the way genuine grievance escalates.
Each repetition should logically exhaust the complaint, but instead it winds tighter.
And then notice how the list — 'offensively poor, miserably poor, beastly poor' — keeps one-upping itself.
'Beastly poor' is the destination — it's where the comedy tips into something almost feral.
What I find architecturally brilliant is that Dickens lets her say 'I love money' in direct speech — no ironic narrator required.
The character indicts herself, and the author stands back.
There's something more than comedy in that catalogue of poverty, though.
The Wilfers are genuinely poor — and in the 1860s that was not an abstraction.
Being 'degradingly poor' in Dickens's London meant vulnerability to debt law, to destitution, to the workhouse at the end of the road.
So when Bella says she hates poverty, we should resist laughing too quickly — she has reasons.
What makes her morally interesting is that she knows wealth would have 'smoothed away' the absurdities of the Harmon arrangement — and she's right.
Money does smooth things away in this society. That is precisely the problem.
And Dickens doesn't let her off the hook as she gets wealthier — if anything, the narrator grows more sardonic.
There's a tiny, devastating observation the narrator makes once Bella is installed at the Boffins' grand house.
"Yet it was not so very long ago that Bella had been fluttered by the discovery that this same Secretary and lodger seem to like her.
Ah! but the eminently aristocratic mansion and Mrs Boffin's dressmaker had not come into play then."
That 'Ah!' is a knife. The narrator uses it like a sigh of disappointed recognition.
Rokesmith's affection was real and she felt it — until the mansion and the dressmaker arrived and rearranged her priorities.
That 'Ah!' is one of Dickens's great single-syllable interventions.
It's the omniscient narrator stepping forward for one beat — not to lecture, just to register.
The word 'eminently' is doing the ironic heavy lifting — it's the narrator mimicking the language of social aspiration while quietly mocking it.
And notice what's been displaced: genuine human feeling, replaced by a mansion and a dressmaker.
The architecture of that sentence makes the exchange obscene — and funny — in equal measure.
James, I want to bring you in here — because Bella's most excruciating moment of self-examination is still to come, and it has a very particular staging.
Yes — the mirror scene in chapter thirty-eight is one of the most peculiar pieces of moral comedy in the novel.
Boffin has been pressing his mercenary philosophy on Bella — and she agrees with it entirely, in her heart.
And yet she finds herself disgusted by him for saying what she privately believes.
She retreats to her room and interrogates herself in the looking-glass — which Dickens uses as a recurring device for Bella's self-confrontations.
The passage is worth reading at length, because the logic is genuinely strange.
"What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure.
It is only what I often say to myself.
Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.
Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?"
She convicts herself in her own court — and the verdict is delivered to a mirror.
'Inconsistent little Beast' — that phrase lands like a slap she administers to herself.
And it echoes later — quite literally — when Bella catches herself measuring everything against Lizzie Hexam's selfless love.
There's a moment that is almost slapstick in its penitential energy.
"There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?"
And she gives herself — Dickens's phrase is exact — 'a penitential poke in the side.'
It's ridiculous. And it's also the beginning of something real happening in her character.
The self-administered poke is a masterpiece of comic craft — but it also solves a narrative problem.
Dickens needs us to believe Bella is capable of transformation without sentimentalising her too early.
Making her physically punish herself — and making it funny — keeps her at an ironic distance even as we start to root for her.
The satirical narrator and the sympathetic narrator are working simultaneously — which is an extraordinarily hard thing to sustain.
What completes the picture, for me, is what Lizzie sees in Bella — or rather, what Bella overhears about herself.
Lizzie describes what she sees in the fire, and what she sees is a character Bella hasn't yet become — but will.
"A heart well worth winning, and well won.
A heart that, once won, goes through fire and water for the winner, and never changes, and is never daunted."
Lizzie is reading Bella's potential, not her present self — and that generosity is what begins to change her.
It's a form of moral credit extended to someone who hasn't yet earned it — and that is a very particular kind of grace.
The rhythm of that sentence is extraordinary — 'never changes, and is never daunted' — it has the cadence of a vow.
And Dickens gives it to Lizzie — the character with the least social power in the room — as if worth and perception are inversely related to position.
Bella, who has spent the novel measuring everything in money, is measured here in something else entirely.
And she feels it. The penitential poke is funny — but this moment is tender.
That movement — from self-mockery to something genuinely tender — is exactly what makes Bella one of Dickens's most alive characters.
We've been tracing her from that first furious speech about orange chips, through the mirror's uncomfortable verdicts, to Lizzie's extraordinary gift of faith.
In our next segment, we'll look at the novel's other great moral test — the dust heaps, and what money made from waste does to the souls who inherit it.

segments.title: The Machinery of Poverty: How Dickens Built His Critique

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously as the extraordinary work of art and moral argument it is.
Each episode, we take a section of the book apart — the craft, the history, the experience of reading — and put it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm joined today by three people whose company I find genuinely indispensable when thinking about this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with total attention to how every gear fits.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions were, how they worked, and who they crushed.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel who came to it as a teenager and has never quite left.
Today's segment is called The Machinery of Poverty: How Dickens Built His Critique.
We're going to look at how Dickens attacks the institutions that fail the poor — the schools, the workhouses, the Poor Law — and how he does it with both fury and extraordinary comic precision.
Eleanor, the school passage is one of the most remarkable pieces of satirical writing in the whole novel.
What's Dickens actually doing there, architecturally speaking?
What strikes me first is the sheer accumulation — Dickens builds his satirical case the way a prosecutor builds a charge sheet.
He gives us this school that is nominally for moral improvement, and then proceeds to demolish every pretension it has, detail by excruciating detail.
The central target is what he calls — and it's a magnificent phrase — 'a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil was childish and innocent.'
'A grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil was childish and innocent.'
That pairing — grimly and ludicrous — is doing everything at once.
It's funny and it's horrifying and it refuses to let you choose between those responses.
Then he gives us Little Margery — this absurd, pious fairy-tale child forced on women who have lived actual brutal lives.
The comedy there is almost baroque in its elaboration, but the cruelty underneath it is absolutely serious.
And then the prose itself enacts the chaos it's describing.
That sentence — the best quote in the whole passage — is one I have read aloud to anyone who'll sit still long enough.
'An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.'
The repetition of 'jumbled' four times and then once more — it's incantatory.
It's a spell, a hex, cast on the whole institution.
And then he goes further — the Sunday school section with the 'chief executioner' and the 'acolyte' smoothing children's faces.
That word 'smooth' — applied to a hot hand silencing a child — is quietly one of the most sinister things in the book.
The executioner imagery is pointed in a very specific historical direction.

These ragged schools and charity schools of the 1860s were genuinely contested terrain — some reformers saw them as the thin edge of emancipation, and others, including Dickens, saw them as instruments of social control dressed in piety.
The moral literature he mocks — Thomas Twopence, Little Margery — that genre was real, and it was pernicious precisely in the way he identifies.
Its message, as Dickens puts it with wonderful precision, is that you were to do good 'not because it was good, but because you were to make a good thing of it.'
'Not because it was good, but because you were to make a good thing of it.'
That is a diagnosis of Victorian philanthropic culture that holds up with uncomfortable force today.
James, that connects directly to something Dickens does with the Boffins — which is to set genuine moral seriousness against all that performative virtue.
There's a passage where Dickens reflects on the Boffins' journey through life guided by what he calls 'a religious sense of duty and desire to do right.'
And then comes this extraordinary sentence: 'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
Six words at the end — 'but Good, never' — and the whole periodic structure collapses into that monosyllable.
It's the opposite of the school's moral literature — not transactional virtue, not reward, just Good, persisting on its own terms.
And it makes the Betty Higden passages all the more devastating by contrast.
Because Betty Higden is exactly that kind of persistent goodness — and the system breaks her.
The passage where Dickens describes what official cruelty has done to her inner life — it's one of the most haunting things I've ever read.
'To conceal herself in sickness, like a lower animal; to creep out of sight and coil herself away and die; had become this woman's instinct.'
She has been so thoroughly degraded by institutional cruelty that self-concealment has replaced self-preservation.
And to hide a sick child from help — Dickens calls that her 'idea of maternal love.' The irony is so cold it burns.
What Dickens is documenting there is not metaphor — it is observable social behaviour produced by the New Poor Law of 1834.
The law was deliberately designed to be repellent — the principle of 'less eligibility' meant conditions in the workhouse had to be worse than the worst free labour.
The consequence was exactly what Dickens describes in the later passage — destitute people choosing exposure and starvation over entering the institution.
And Dickens makes the political address entirely explicit — 'my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards' — he's not writing a novel, he's delivering a parliamentary indictment.

The passage builds to this: 'when we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us —'
'it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance.'
Two hundred years of parliamentary rhetoric has not produced a more precise account of systemic failure.
The rhetorical strategy in that passage is something I find technically astonishing.
Dickens uses that repeated address — 'my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards' — as a kind of battering ram.
Each time it recurs, the irony has thickened slightly — it begins as formal address and ends as pure contempt.
And 'the Gospel according to Podsnappery' is one of his finest coinages — naming the entire ideological system that refuses to see suffering as real.
Podsnap is the character who won't discuss anything unpleasant — and here his name becomes an 'ism', a whole world-view, in a single coinage.
The passage about Betty wandering and witnessing — the passage about the 'appointed evader of the public trust' — is where I feel the gothic register breaking through.
She moves through a landscape of suffering like a figure in a nightmare.

Dickens writes: 'she would light upon the shameful spectacle of some desolate creature — or some wretched ragged groups of either sex, with children among them, huddled together like the smaller vermin for a little warmth.'
'Huddled together like the smaller vermin for a little warmth.'
Calling them 'the smaller vermin' — that's the language of the system speaking, not Dickens.
He's adopting their dehumanising vocabulary to expose it.
And then she encounters 'the appointed evader of the public trust' doing 'his dirty office' — that phrase 'dirty office' is exactly right, bureaucratic and soiled at once.
The 'Relieving Officer' — which is what that evader actually was — had discretionary power to turn away applicants, and abuse of that discretion was endemic.
Dickens knew this because he followed the cases in the newspapers — and in the later authorial address he cites The Lancet directly.
In the postscript passage he sets out his view of the Poor Law with the careful precision of a lawyer presenting evidence.
He writes: 'I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised.'

'In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity — and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.'
'Known language could say no more' — that is a legal formulation, and he means it exactly.
He is not being rhetorical — he is making a precise claim that the administration of this law was, in measurable cases, also criminal.
What I keep coming back to is the formal audacity of embedding all of this inside a novel.
Dickens doesn't separate the social critique from the fiction — he fuses them.
Betty Higden's death isn't just moving — it's evidential.
And the school scene isn't just satirical — it's also a precise argument about how ideology reproduces itself through children.
The form is doing the work of the argument at every level — structure, sentence, image, rhythm.
That's a beautiful place to mark the scale of what Dickens is attempting — a novel that is simultaneously art, testimony, and legal brief.
And I think what this conversation has shown is that he earns every register he inhabits — the comic grotesque, the gothic, the polemical — because they are all in service of the same moral claim.
We'll be back shortly to look at how the novel's characters navigate — and sometimes escape — the machinery we've been discussing.

segments.title: A Man Unmade: Identity and the Plot of Substitution

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're in the heart of the novel's great secret — John Harmon, the man who is dead and not dead, known and unknown, himself and not himself.
It is one of the most audacious identity plots in all of Victorian fiction, and we want to pull it apart — the craft, the psychology, the moral stakes.
Eleanor Hartley is our literary critic and novelist — she's going to lead us through the architecture of how Dickens constructed this.
James Blackstone brings the social and legal historian's eye — what does it actually mean, in this world, to be declared dead?
And Caroline Woodcourt, our close reader, who I suspect has very strong feelings about what Harmon puts everyone through.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because Dickens actually steps in, quite unusually, to tell us what he was doing with this character.
Yes, and it is a remarkable authorial intrusion — Dickens speaking in his own voice, mid-novel, to defend his artistic choices.
He's essentially saying to the reader: you think I'm being obscure, but I am being deliberate.
Listen to the precision of how he puts it.

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
The antithesis of 'conceal' and 'suggest' in that single clause is extraordinary.
He's not hiding Harmon's identity — he's constantly gesturing at it, trusting the reader to feel the outline of the shape before they can name it.
That is a fundamentally different relationship with suspense than, say, the pure mystery plot.
It's dramatic irony rather than withholding — and the effect on the reader is one of creeping recognition rather than sudden revelation.
And there's a real-world weight behind that 'not slain' that I don't think we should pass over too quickly.
To be wanted by the police, plastered on the walls of London as a missing person — that is a legally and socially catastrophic position.
The passage in chapter thirty-one makes this chillingly clear.

'When the snare into which he fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly accepted the aid that fell upon him.'
'Placarded by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead' — that phrase carries the full machinery of mid-Victorian public order.
Once the coroner's process and the police broadsheets have spoken, you are officially a corpse, whatever your own heartbeat says.
Harmon hasn't chosen to be dead — the institutional apparatus has chosen it for him, and he's stumbled into accepting it.
What arrests me is the physical choreography of the scene where all three identities collapse into one body.
It's almost comic — oakum hair and whiskers stuffed into a coat in a moment, a solitary street, a favourable wind.
And then this sentence, which I find genuinely haunting.
'Yet in that same moment he was the Secretary also, Mr Boffin's Secretary. For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world.'
'Lost, wanted' — those two words are doing so much.
He is lost to society and to himself, and wanted by the police — but also simply wanted, yearned for, in the deeper sense.
Dickens stacks the identities like coats being pulled off, and they all belong to the same cold, uncertain man.
That repetition — 'as never man was like another in this world' — is the verbal hinge of the whole passage.
It's used twice, almost identically, and that formal echo is Dickens's way of showing that the three names are one thing, not three.
The sentence structure enacts the identity collapse that the plot is about.
But what floors me is the passage where Harmon tries to narrate his own unconscious state — the moment where self dissolves entirely.
He reaches a logical impasse that is also a philosophical one.
'Still correct, with the exception that I cannot possibly express it to myself without using the word I. But it was not I. There was no such thing as I, within my knowledge.'
This is years before Nietzsche, decades before the Modernist dissolution of the self — and here is Dickens finding the grammatical crack in first-person consciousness.
You cannot narrate a self that wasn't there, and yet narrative demands a subject.
That observation has a social dimension too, which I think Eleanor's reading opens up beautifully.
The chapter thirty-one passage makes it explicit: the deception was seeded not by cunning but by damage.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Never yet for good within his knowledge' — that is the indictment of inherited wealth that drives the entire novel.
Harmon has never seen his father's money do anything but corrupt, diminish, and enslave.
So the deception isn't really deception — it's the action of a man trying to find an exit from a world where money determines every human relationship.
I don't entirely let him off the hook, though.
Because the passage where he decides to 'prove Bella' — that is a man performing a test on another human being without her knowledge or consent.
And Dickens gives it to us in Harmon's own words, lying in a sickbed, making a calculation.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Turning the danger to the account of proving Bella' — there is something cold in that phrasing.
He's treating near-death as an opportunity, and treating Bella as a problem to be solved rather than a person to be known.
James is right that the money has warped everything — but it has warped Harmon too.
That's a vital corrective, and I think the novel actually holds both things simultaneously — sympathy and judgement.
The chapter thirty-one passage ends with a trap from which there is no clean exit.
If he comes to life and accepts the inheritance, he has to buy Bella.
If he rejects it, he punishes her.
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?' — that binary is the moral architecture of the whole Harmon plot.
Every deception that follows — the Secretary, the disguise, the long watching — flows from that impossible double bind.
What strikes me, bringing those threads together, is how thoroughly Dickens implicates the reader in Harmon's position.
We too have been watching Bella without her knowledge, making our own assessments of her character.
That authorial note about concealment and suggestion — Dickens is inviting us to be, in some sense, co-conspirators.

In our next segment, we'll move from the man who won't be named to the woman at the centre of his scheme — Bella Wilfer, and the question of whether she passes the test, or whether the test itself is the problem.

segments.title: The Heart Beneath the Gold: Bella's Redemption and Voice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great obsession with money and what it does to people.
Now we turn to the character who sits at the centre of that argument: Bella Wilfer.
Her arc — from frank mercenary ambition to something altogether harder won — is one of the novel's most debated achievements.
With me today: Dr Eleanor Hartley, who will be watching how Dickens engineers that transformation on the level of the sentence itself.
Prof James Blackstone, whose eye for social and moral context will keep us honest about what Bella is actually choosing.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt, who has read and re-read these pages with enormous affection and some strong opinions about what Bella deserves.
James, let's begin with you — because R. Wilfer's account of his daughter's moral turning point is extraordinary.
What do you make of Dickens routing Bella's great renunciation through the voice of the Cherub?
It's a characteristically shrewd move, and I think it often doesn't get the credit it deserves.
R. Wilfer is the novel's great figure of cheerful, dignified poverty — and Dickens gives him this moment.
He becomes the unexpected vehicle for articulating what Bella's transformation actually means in moral terms.
And notice the language he uses — it has that tremendous Dickensian rhythmic accumulation.

"this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive?"
"For any price that could be paid to her by any one alive" — that is not sentiment.
That is a rigorous moral statement dressed in the Cherub's warmly comic syntax.
Dickens is also being very precise about what Bella is refusing: not wealth itself, but the sale of ethical judgment for wealth.
The anaphora in that sentence is doing so much heavy lifting.
"What was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust" — each pairing is a complete moral coordinate.
Dickens is constructing a whole ethical compass through pure repetition of syntactic form.
And what I love is that it's framed as a question — "Am I leading up to it right?"
The Cherub's characteristic tentativeness actually mimics the reader's own uncertain hope for Bella.
We've been unsure whether to trust her change — and here is her father, also slightly unsure, also checking.
It's delicate and it's perfect.
What strikes me every time I read those scenes is how hard Bella is working to be believed.
Not just by the other characters — by the reader.
There's a moment where she says to John, and I think it's the most genuinely vulnerable line she has in the whole novel —
"Try me through some reverse, John—try me through some trial—and tell them after that, what you think of me."
She's not asking for comfort or reassurance.
She's asking for the test — asking to be put through something difficult precisely because she knows easy virtue proves nothing.
That's a quite remarkable degree of self-knowledge for a character who started out with almost none.
And the reversal of conventional romance logic is quite pointed there, isn't it.
The traditional heroine waits for her circumstances to improve so her true nature can shine through.
Bella is essentially demanding poverty as a proving ground — which is exactly what she fled at the start.
In social terms, that's a complete inversion of the novel's opening position for her.
It also sets up that remarkable revelation scene, where we finally understand the full architecture of Mr Boffin's scheme.
Because when Bella pieces it together herself and confronts Boffin — that speech is astonishing to read as a piece of construction.
She is essentially writing the novel's own thesis back to its perpetrator.
Caroline, you have the passage — I'd love you to take that quote.
Gladly, because this is the passage I've been wanting to get to since we started.
Bella has worked it all out — Boffin's pretended corruption, the whole painful performance — and she puts it to him directly.

"This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in; but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking."
That is the sentence she puts in Boffin's mouth — those words he said to himself about her.
"This shallow creature."
She is quoting the worst assessment of herself back to the man who held it — and she's done it without flinching.
That takes a kind of courage that I find genuinely moving every time.
And note that she is holding him prisoner by the coat with both hands as she does it.
Dickens gives her a physical grip on the moment that is almost theatrical.
She will not let go until she has named every element of what was done — and why.
In social terms, a young woman of her position grabbing a wealthy patron's coat and demanding an accounting is a radical act.
What I keep coming back to is how the passage positions Bella's intelligence as the very instrument of her redemption.
Boffin's gamble — the whole calculated cruelty of his performance — rested on her being smart enough to read it correctly.
And she is.
That's not a small thing to grant a female character in a mid-Victorian novel.
And then comes the passage that undoes me completely, every single time.
Because she has just performed this extraordinary act of comprehension — and then immediately turns to confess what she cannot comprehend.

"It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife."
"A little better."
Not transformed, not redeemed, not purified — just a little better.
The modesty of that is heartbreaking and honest in equal measure.
And "very very grateful" — Dickens doesn't reach for a grandiloquent word there.
He gives her the simplest possible register, doubled.
After all the rhetorical fireworks of her confrontation with Boffin, that plainness lands harder than anything ornate could.
The oscillation between those two registers — the rhetorically brilliant Bella and the simply grateful Bella — is what makes her feel like a person rather than a lesson.
Redemption arcs in fiction so often flatten the character at the moment of resolution.
Dickens keeps both the wit and the vulnerability in the room at the same time.
That seems to me exactly the right place to rest for a moment — that image of Bella holding both things at once.
Clever and humble, fully formed and still becoming.
Coming up, we'll move from Bella's interior life to the world around her — the river, the dust heaps, and the economic machinery that makes her story possible.
Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — slowly, carefully, with real pleasure.
Each week we bring together three exceptional readers to work through the novel's most charged moments.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is riveted by the architecture of fiction — how a structural choice can carry an entire chapter's moral weight.
Prof James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions looked like from the inside — and what it cost people to inhabit them.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and who loves nothing more than reading a sentence aloud until it gives up its secrets.
Today's segment sits at the heart of everything the novel is doing with identity and concealment.
John Harmon — legally dead, living under an assumed name — has been watching his own life from the outside.
We're going to look at what Dickens is up to with that disguise, what it costs his characters, and what it reveals about the novel's deepest design.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because Dickens himself breaks the fourth wall to defend this plot, and I think that's where we have to start.
Yes — and it's a remarkable moment, because Dickens steps entirely outside the fiction to speak as the craftsman at his bench.
He's not apologising for the complexity of the plot — he's claiming it as a deliberate artistic achievement.
Listen to the precision of the phrasing — he writes:

"To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design."
That phrase — "always working itself out" — is doing extraordinary work.
The secret isn't inert — it's a living force threading through every chapter, pressing against the narrative surface.
And then he offers this beautiful image — the story-weaver at the loom, the whole pattern visible to him, invisible to the reader until the cloth is finished.
That image of weaving captures something essential about how the Harmon disguise functions structurally — every scene with Rokesmith is a hidden thread.
The weaving metaphor is apt, but I want to pull on one of those threads from a different angle.
When Harmon explains the scheme to us in his confession, he is describing something that would have struck a Victorian reader as both understandable and deeply irregular.
He dresses as a common sailor — an act of class transgression, not merely disguise — in order to surveil a woman he is contractually betrothed to.
The passage spells this out quite plainly — he sets up the scheme as follows:

"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way"
The word "plot" is quite deliberate — Harmon uses it of himself, as if he already half-knows he is the villain of someone else's story.
And notice what he says when nothing comes of it: "I should be no worse off."
He is calculating risk like a man who holds all the legal cards — because, under the inheritance law of the period, he entirely does.
What strikes me reading that passage is how Harmon keeps interrupting his own confession to verify it.
He says: "I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right."
He is conducting a cross-examination of himself — as if he doesn't quite trust his own account of his own life.
And that connects directly to the gothic strangeness of the chapter Eleanor has, where Rokesmith literally lies awake burying John Harmon overnight.
Dickens calls it "the sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon all night long."
A sexton digs graves — so Rokesmith is both the gravedigger and the corpse.
The tenderness of that image is what gets me every time — there's grief in it, not just ingenuity.
Caroline's put her finger on something I find technically extraordinary about that passage.
Dickens gives us both Harmon and Rokesmith simultaneously — one being buried, one doing the burying — in a single character's consciousness.
And then he resolves that doubled self into a single, devastating image.

"No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place."
The ghost looks on at its own former life — that is the essence of Harmon's position throughout the novel.
He watches Bella fall in love with Rokesmith never knowing she is falling in love with the man she was contracted to marry.
The disguise is not an evasion of the inheritance plot — it is the only way Dickens can morally validate its outcome.
I'll grant Dickens the moral ingenuity — but I want to register a mild dissent about whether the test is as clean as the novel pretends.
Harmon engineers Bella's circumstances — he is the reason she is poor, the reason she is dependent, the reason she is tested at all.
And this is explicit in his own account — he describes his confederate Radfoot's story as having "God only knows how much of it true, and how much of it false."
The entire enterprise rests on a network of deceptions whose moral credibility Harmon never fully reckons with.
Dickens resolves it tenderly — but the social historian in me notes that the man with all the money and all the information also controls the terms of the verdict.
James is right to push on that — and yet I find I can't quite sustain the critique when I'm actually inside the prose.
Because Dickens doesn't let Harmon off the hook, exactly — he lets him haunt himself.
That phrase — "the state of existence out of which it had departed" — is heartbreaking in its passivity.
Rokesmith doesn't choose to re-enter life — he chooses to remove himself from it, again, on moral grounds.
That's a kind of self-punishment that the novel takes very seriously — even if we might interrogate its premises, as James suggests.
What I hear in all three of your readings is that the disguise plot operates on several registers at once — craft, ethics, psychology, and class — and Dickens is juggling all of them.
Eleanor's loom image — Dickens's own — keeps coming back to me: the pattern only legible once the cloth is whole.
And yet James's point stands — the man holding the shuttle also determines what pattern gets woven.
In our next segment, we'll follow those threads into the Boffin household — where another kind of performance is underway, and where the moral stakes become, if anything, even harder to read.

segments.title: What Remains: Society, Dust, and the Novel's Final Word

utterances.text: We come now to our final segment — and perhaps the most far-reaching.
Our Mutual Friend ends, as it began, with questions about what society does with its waste — its dust, its dead, its discarded people.
James, you've been waiting to talk about Dickens's most directly polemical passages, and I think now is the moment.
Thank you — yes, because what's remarkable about this novel is that Dickens doesn't confine his social critique to implication or allegory.
At certain moments he turns directly to face the governing classes, names them, and delivers what can only be called a warning.
There's a passage centred on the dustheap — that great mountain of ash and refuse — where Dickens addresses his reader with startling directness.
"My lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, when you in the course of your dust-shovelling and cinder-raking have piled up a mountain of pretentious failure,"
"you must off with your honourable coats for the removal of it, and fall to the work with the power of all the queen's horses and all the queen's men, or it will come rushing down and bury us alive."
The nursery rhyme cadence — Humpty Dumpty, the king's horses — is unmistakable, and entirely deliberate.
Dickens is telling the establishment: you have built this ruin yourselves, and only you can clear it — and the clock is running.
What I find extraordinary is how that rhetoric is earned — structurally, I mean.
The dustheap isn't introduced at the end of the novel as a symbol — it's present from the very first pages, physically dominating the landscape.
So by the time Dickens turns on the governing classes and demands they clear it, every reader has been living with that image for hundreds of pages.
The rhetorical impact is inseparable from the architectural patience that preceded it.
And notice the subtle comedy in 'honourable coats' — the suggestion that to actually do the work would require these men to abandon their dignity, their office, their pretence.
And the imagery of waste runs even deeper than the dustheaps — there's a passage about wastepaper blowing through London's streets that I find almost unbearably pointed.
Dickens contrasts London, where scraps of paper blow everywhere uncollected, with Paris — and the comparison is deliberately unflattering.
"In Paris, where nothing is wasted, costly and luxurious city though it be, but where wonderful human ants creep out of holes and pick up every scrap, there is no such thing."
The phrase 'wonderful human ants' is extraordinary — it holds admiration and pity in the same breath.
These are people so poor that starvation sharpens their senses — 'sharp eyes and sharp stomachs reap even the east wind' — and Dickens wants you to feel both their ingenuity and their desperation.
That passage arrests me every time — because it's so quick, so almost casual, and yet it contains the entire moral argument of the novel in miniature.
London wastes. The poor of Paris cannot afford to.
And the wind that blows the wastepaper about London is the same east wind that Paris's poor manage to extract something from — that detail is devastating.
It connects directly to Betty Higden's funeral — that scene in the unmarked churchyard, where Dickens makes his most personal plea.
He writes: "It might not be to do an unreasonably great deal for the diggers and hewers, in a registering age, if we ticketed their graves at the common charge;"
"so that a new generation might know which was which."
The word 'ticketed' is so precise — so pointedly administrative — in a novel drowning in bureaucracy that discards people.
And Dickens doesn't let the sentiment become easy — he anticipates the objection immediately.
He writes — and I love this — 'It would be sentimental, perhaps?'
"But how say ye, my lords and gentleman and honourable boards, shall we not find good standing-room left for a little sentiment, if we look into our crowds?"
He weaponizes the word 'sentimental' — turns the accusation back on those who would use it to dismiss the poor.
If the charge is sentiment, Dickens accepts it — and then asks whether there's room for it, which is a far more dangerous question.
What's historically interesting is that Dickens is writing at precisely the moment when the registering age he mentions — civil registration, census-taking — was being consolidated.
The state was suddenly very good at counting the poor, classifying them, administering them — and yet their graves remained unmarked, their deaths unrecorded in any humane way.
That bureaucratic efficiency deployed in the service of indifference is exactly what made Dickens furious — and it's the same fury that powers that address to the honourable boards.
I want to bring in one more passage before we close — because I think the novel's treatment of the individual is as important as its treatment of society.
The scene where Bella confronts Mr Boffin about what he was really doing — showing her the corrupting face of wealth deliberately — is one of the most tender moments in the book.
She tells him what she believes he was thinking — and Dickens gives her the words to say it.

"You showed her, in yourself, the most detestable sides of wealth, saying in your own mind, 'This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in;"
"but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking.'"
The phrase 'a glaring instance' — that's the novel itself, isn't it?
Dickens holding up the dustheaps, the Veneerings, the tide of rumour, the unmarked graves — all of it a glaring instance kept before us.
That's beautifully put — and it connects to something I keep thinking about with this novel's structure.
There's that extraordinary passage early on — the tidal metaphor for how news of the Harmon murder circulates — and it prefigures everything.
"Like the tides on which it had been borne to the knowledge of men, the Harmon Murder went up and down, and ebbed and flowed,"
"now in the town, now in the country, now among palaces, now among hovels, now among lords and ladies and gentlefolks, now among labourers and hammerers and ballast-heavers,"
"until at last, after a long interval of slack water it got out to sea and drifted away."
The list — palaces and hovels, lords and ballast-heavers — is the whole social world held momentarily in one sentence before the tide takes it.
And the ending — 'got out to sea and drifted away' — that's both a release and a warning about forgetting.
The novel refuses to let things drift, though — that's what separates it from mere entertainment.
The tides carry the Harmon murder away into public forgetfulness, but the dustheap keeps accumulating.
'Making little or no daily impression on the heap of ashes, though as the days passed on, the heap was seen to be slowly melting' — it changes on its own terms, not ours.
That's what makes the warning so urgent: social problems don't wait for polite attention.
That seems to me the perfect note on which to end — the dustheap doesn't wait.
What Our Mutual Friend gives us is a novel that holds an entire society in solution — river and shore, palace and hovel, gold and ash — and asks what we choose to see.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — it has been a privilege to think alongside you about this extraordinary novel.
For Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, thank you for listening.

c3:p42.text:
The low building had the look of having once been a mill. There was a
      rotten wart of wood upon its forehead that seemed to indicate where the
      sails had been, but the whole was very indistinctly seen in the obscurity
      of the night. The boy lifted the latch of the door, and they passed at
      once into a low circular room, where a man stood before a red fire,
      looking down into it, and a girl sat engaged in needlework. The fire was
      in a rusty brazier, not fitted to the hearth; and a common lamp, shaped
      like a hyacinth-root, smoked and flared in the neck of a stone bottle on
      the table. There was a wooden bunk or berth in a corner, and in another
      corner a wooden stair leading above—so clumsy and steep that it was
      little better than a ladder. Two or three old sculls and oars stood
      against the wall, and against another part of the wall was a small
      dresser, making a spare show of the commonest articles of crockery and
      cooking-vessels. The roof of the room was not plastered, but was formed of
      the flooring of the room above. This, being very old, knotted, seamed, and
      beamed, gave a lowering aspect to the chamber; and roof, and walls, and
      floor, alike abounding in old smears of flour, red-lead (or some such
      stain which it had probably acquired in warehousing), and damp, alike had
      a look of decomposition.
c3:p42.summary: Dickens describes Gaffer's old mill-house in vivid detail: its rotting exterior, the low circular interior with rusty brazier and smoking lamp, wooden berth and steep stair, scattered oars and simple crockery, and its pervasive atmosphere of decay and damp staining.

c34:p0.text:
It was a foggy day in London, and the fog was heavy and dark. Animate
      London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing,
      and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose
      between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.
      Gaslights flared in the shops with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing
      themselves to be night-creatures that had no business abroad under the
      sun; while the sun itself when it was for a few moments dimly indicated
      through circling eddies of fog, showed as if it had gone out and were
      collapsing flat and cold. Even in the surrounding country it was a foggy
      day, but there the fog was grey, whereas in London it was, at about the
      boundary line, dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then
      browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City—which call
      Saint Mary Axe—it was rusty-black. From any point of the high ridge
      of land northward, it might have been discerned that the loftiest
      buildings made an occasional struggle to get their heads above the foggy
      sea, and especially that the great dome of Saint Paul’s seemed to die
      hard; but this was not perceivable in the streets at their feet, where the
      whole metropolis was a heap of vapour charged with muffled sound of
      wheels, and enfolding a gigantic catarrh.
c34:p0.summary: A richly detailed description of heavy London fog that obscures the city, making it simultaneously visible and invisible, with vivid imagery of gaslight, collapsed sun, and the metropolis transformed into vaporous chaos.
c34:p0.best_quote: Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.

Day was breaking at Plashwater Weir Mill Lock. Stars were yet visible, but
      there was dull light in the east that was not the light of night. The moon
      had gone down, and a mist crept along the banks of the river, seen through
      which the trees were the ghosts of trees, and the water was the ghost of
      water. This earth looked spectral, and so did the pale stars: while the
      cold eastern glare, expressionless as to heat or colour, with the eye of
      the firmament quenched, might have been likened to the stare of the dead.

c4:p48.text:
‘You are a chit and a little idiot,’ returned Bella, ‘or you wouldn’t make
      such a dolly speech. What did you expect me to do? Wait till you are a
      woman, and don’t talk about what you don’t understand. You only show your
      ignorance!’ Then, whimpering again, and at intervals biting the curls, and
      stopping to look how much was bitten off, ‘It’s a shame! There never was
      such a hard case! I shouldn’t care so much if it wasn’t so ridiculous. It
      was ridiculous enough to have a stranger coming over to marry me, whether
      he liked it or not. It was ridiculous enough to know what an embarrassing
      meeting it would be, and how we never could pretend to have an inclination
      of our own, either of us. It was ridiculous enough to know I shouldn’t
      like him—how  could  I like him, left to him in a will, like a dozen
      of spoons, with everything cut and dried beforehand, like orange chips.
      Talk of orange flowers indeed! I declare again it’s a shame! Those
      ridiculous points would have been smoothed away by the money, for I love
      money, and want money—want it dreadfully. I hate to be poor, and we
      are degradingly poor, offensively poor, miserably poor, beastly poor. But
      here I am, left with all the ridiculous parts of the situation remaining,
      and, added to them all, this ridiculous dress! And if the truth was known,
      when the Harmon murder was all over the town, and people were speculating
      on its being suicide, I dare say those impudent wretches at the clubs and
      places made jokes about the miserable creature’s having preferred a watery
      grave to me. It’s likely enough they took such liberties; I shouldn’t
      wonder! I declare it’s a very hard case indeed, and I am a most
      unfortunate girl. The idea of being a kind of a widow, and never having
      been married! And the idea of being as poor as ever after all, and going
      into black, besides, for a man I never saw, and should have hated—as
      far as  he  was concerned—if I had seen!’
c4:p48.summary: Bella unleashes a torrent of complaint: the arranged marriage to a stranger was absurd, his death was embarrassing, and now she is stuck mourning him in ridiculous black dress while remaining poor. She passionately declares her love of money and her horror at their degrading poverty, then suggests people mocked her for the Harmon's suicide (presumably), and concludes that being a 'widow' who was never married is the ultimate injustice.

It was ridiculous enough to know what an embarrassing meeting it would be, and how we never could pretend to have an inclination of our own, either of us. It was ridiculous enough to know I shouldn't like him—how could I like him, left to him in a will, like a dozen of spoons, with everything cut and dried beforehand, like orange chips.

c18:p1.text:
It was a school for all ages, and for both sexes. The latter were kept
      apart, and the former were partitioned off into square assortments. But,
      all the place was pervaded by a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil
      was childish and innocent. This pretence, much favoured by the
      lady-visitors, led to the ghastliest absurdities. Young women old in the
      vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves
      enthralled by the good child’s book, the Adventures of Little Margery, who
      resided in the village cottage by the mill; severely reproved and morally
      squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty; divided her
      porridge with singing birds; denied herself a new nankeen bonnet, on the
      ground that the turnips did not wear nankeen bonnets, neither did the
      sheep who ate them; who plaited straw and delivered the dreariest orations
      to all comers, at all sorts of unseasonable times. So, unwieldy young
      dredgers and hulking mudlarks were referred to the experiences of Thomas
      Twopence, who, having resolved not to rob (under circumstances of uncommon
      atrocity) his particular friend and benefactor, of eighteenpence,
      presently came into supernatural possession of three and sixpence, and
      lived a shining light ever afterwards. (Note, that the benefactor came to
      no good.) Several swaggering sinners had written their own biographies in
      the same strain; it always appearing from the lessons of those very
      boastful persons, that you were to do good, not because it  was  good, but
      because you were to make a good thing of it. Contrariwise, the adult
      pupils were taught to read (if they could learn) out of the New Testament;
      and by dint of stumbling over the syllables and keeping their bewildered
      eyes on the particular syllables coming round to their turn, were as
      absolutely ignorant of the sublime history, as if they had never seen or
      heard of it. An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a
      school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white,
      jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night. And particularly
      every Sunday night. For then, an inclined plane of unfortunate infants
      would be handed over to the prosiest and worst of all the teachers with
      good intentions, whom nobody older would endure. Who, taking his stand on
      the floor before them as chief executioner, would be attended by a
      conventional volunteer boy as executioner’s assistant. When and where it
      first became the conventional system that a weary or inattentive infant in
      a class must have its face smoothed downward with a hot hand, or when and
      where the conventional volunteer boy first beheld such system in
      operation, and became inflamed with a sacred zeal to administer it,
      matters not. It was the function of the chief executioner to hold forth,
      and it was the function of the acolyte to dart at sleeping infants,
      yawning infants, restless infants, whimpering infants, and smooth their
      wretched faces; sometimes with one hand, as if he were anointing them for
      a whisker; sometimes with both hands, applied after the fashion of
      blinkers. And so the jumble would be in action in this department for a
      mortal hour; the exponent drawling on to My Dearert Childerrenerr, let us
      say, for example, about the beautiful coming to the Sepulchre; and
      repeating the word Sepulchre (commonly used among infants) five hundred
      times, and never once hinting what it meant; the conventional boy
      smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole
      hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes,
      whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in
      High Market for the purpose.

      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in

      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its

      got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to
      relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their
      heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is
      a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance. It may not be
      so written in the Gospel according to Podsnappery; you may not ‘find these
      words’ for the text of a sermon, in the Returns of the Board of Trade; but
      they have been the truth since the foundations of the universe were laid,
      and they will be the truth until the foundations of the universe are
      shaken by the Builder. This boastful handiwork of ours, which fails in its
      terrors for the professional pauper, the sturdy breaker of windows and the
      rampant tearer of clothes, strikes with a cruel and a wicked stab at the
      stricken sufferer, and is a horror to the deserving and unfortunate. We

In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.

      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John

      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of

He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.

To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
